images.text:
Kristi: Hi! How are you?
Friend: Good thanks! And you?
Kristi: Great! It's energetic in here, isn't it?
Friend: Yeah! It seems like it's going to be a great event, doesn't it? Here's a map and catalog of the employers.
Kristi: Thanks! I feel like I'm prepared now.
Friend: You need a LOT of preparation before one of these fairs, don't you?
Kristi: Yes. You need to make a good first impression in person. And, you should take the initiative and discern all you can about the employers and industry you are interested in. I also learned the importance of preparing a 30-second introduction speech.

Friend: Sorry? What's that?
Kristi: It's a quick speech that highlights your interests, experience, strengths, accomplishments, and goals. It captures the interest of the person you are attempting to engage.
Friend: That's really important, isn't it? So how do you do it?
Kristi: First you introduce yourself. Then you give a brief description of your current role.
Friend: That could be "a student", couldn't it?
Kristi: Sure! Then you highlight what you could bring to the company, based on your experience and skills. You need to end with a question that shows you have done some research about the company. It should be prepared in advance, but shouldn't sound memorized. I'm going to deliver mine for the first time right now!
Friend: Good luck!

Kristi: Good morning. My name is Kristy Lenard. I've just finished a two-year internship as a copy editor at Polygon. It was a great experience and I was able to put my English degree from Harvard to good use. I'm a skilled editor and writer and I thrive under tight deadlines and multiple projects. For me, relaxation comes in the form of cycling and singing in a choir. I've read that this company is moving to a new digital format. Could you tell me a little bit more about that?

contents.value: It's important to follow some rules when you give an introduction speech. First, you should introduce yourself. Next, you want to give a brief description of your current occupation, which could be a job or you could be student. Then you highlight the experience and skills that you could bring to the company. At the end, you should ask a question about the company that shows that you have researched it. It's best not to memorize your speech. You want to sound prepared, but natural.

Intonation of Question Tags and Short Questions
You can use rising and falling intonation to give meaning to your statements.
When a tag is spoken, the voice can go up or down. If the voice goes up, it is called rising intonation and if it goes down, it is called falling intonation.
<span class="italic">It's energetic in here, isn't it? ↘
You use falling intonation when you are sure (or almost sure) that your statement is true. You know that it is energetic in the job fair. The tag is not a real question.
You use falling intonation to invite someone to continue the conversation.
<span class="italic">That could be a student, couldn't it? ↗

A rising intonation means that the speaker is less sure. You think that an employment role could be “student”, but you aren't sure. The tag is more like a real question. You want your friend to confirm whether or not you are correct.
Short statements can be made into questions by using rising intonation.
You? ↗ means “How about you?” You use this to ask the same question back to someone.

For example:
‘How was your weekend?”
“Great! You?”
You also use rising intonation to give a different meaning to words like sorry and excuse me.

Sorry. ↘ means “I apologize.”
Sorry? ↗ means “I didn't hear you. Please repeat.”

Excuse me. ↘ means “Please move.” or “I need to interrupt.”
Excuse me? ↗ means “I didn't hear you.” or “I can't believe what you just said!”
There's lots of energy here, isn't there?  ↘
Good thanks! And you? ↗
You need a LOT of preparation before one of these fairs, don't you?   ↘
Sorry? ↗  What's that?
That could be student, couldn't it?  ↗
Tag Questions: Negative Tags
You use tag questions to ask for clarification and confirmation.
Question tags are short questions at the end of statements.
They are mainly used in speech when we want to:

• confirm that something is true or not, or
  • to encourage a reply from the person we are speaking to.
Question tags can be positive or negative, depending on the meaning you want to express.

A positive statement is followed by a negative question tag.
Use this when you think the other person will agree by saying ‘yes'.
Note: When the verb in the statement is am, the tag is aren't I. (not amn't I)
For example: <span class="italic">I'm late, aren't I?
You always use the same pronoun in the statement and in the tag.
If the subject is a verb, the tag uses the corresponding pronoun.
For example:

There is a lot of energy here, isn't there?
The job fair is crowded, isn't it?
The speaker is interesting, isn't he?
If the main verb is to be or a modal verb, the tag will be the same.
For all other main verbs, use the tag do/does or did/didn't. Look at the examples in the chart.
